accuracy.evidence: Sun heights come from the standard formula sin(alt) = sin(lat)sin(dec) + cos(lat)cos(dec)cos(H) with dec ±23.44° (solstices), no refraction, recomputed in Python: London 51.5° N on 21 June gives 61.9° at midday, −15.1° at midnight and 16 of 24 hourly samples lit (about 16.4 h; real London day length about 16 h 38 min with refraction); North Pole altitude equals the declination all day (+23.44° in June, −23.44° in December). Polar day/night length at the pole (about six months each, with weeks of twilight) checked against NOAA/Met Office explainers. Times labelled as sun time in the adult text.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented children's ideas about day, night and seasons (Vosniadou & Brewer 1994; Sharp 1996 primary astronomy; NASA Space Place seasons misconceptions): the Sun 'sets every night everywhere' (step 2 predict 'Gone, below the snow', tag set), the Sun high or 'right overhead' at the pole (tag overhead, m7), seasons from the Sun coming closer or getting hotter (tags closer/hotter, m3), both poles having summer together (tags both/likehome, p5), and polar night as one night (tags onenight/forever, m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% similar to every flagship lab). 708 flagdaylen (bedtime light across the year at home), 719 flagspin (spin Earth for day and night) and 646 flagglobe (find the poles) never put the learner at the pole: here the same 21 June is replayed at 51.5° N and at 90° N on a 24-hour drag strip, the Sun's computed path stays above the horizon all day, and the tilted globe shows the pole dot staying lit or dark through a full spin. The polar day/night mechanism could not be relabelled for another topic.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees the contrast before it is named: dragging the home day shows sunrise and sunset and grey night hours on the strip; the same date at the pole leaves every hour light with the Sun circling at a fixed low height, and December leaves every hour dark under stars. The spin task then shows why: in June the pole dot stays on the day side for a whole turn while Home crosses into the night side, and the reverse in December. The sort consolidates home vs polar summer vs polar winter.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong answer the lab disproves: 'Gone, below the snow' for midnight in polar summer (the Sun stays up for all 24 hours), 'Yes, high in the sky' / 'Only for one hour' for lunchtime in polar winter (it never rises), and 'Yes, every night' for whether the North Pole goes dark during a June spin (it stays on the day side). A.reveal reports the prediction in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with tagged wrong answers and feedback naming each slip: set, overhead (the polar Sun stays low), lunch and sunsetw (no sunrise, so no sunset), closer and hotter (Earth leans; the Sun does not move or change), both and likehome (the poles are opposite), allday and alldark (home always has some light and some dark), onenight and forever (months, then the Sun returns). Wrong sorts in the lab give the card's reason, e.g. 'Not at home. Only near the poles in summer…'.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid under 6.5, adult under 9.5). Kid text uses short sentences for ages 5–7 and the precise terms sunrise, sunset, horizon, midnight sun, polar night, North Pole and South Pole, with 'leans' for tilt. Canvas words are short labels (midnight, morning, midday, evening; day side, night side; Sun is below); buttons say exactly what they do (+ 1 hour, Play the whole day, Spin one day).

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases and explanation similarity under 12% to every lesson. The four kid paragraphs carry home day/night, midnight sun, polar night and the lean as the reason; the adult text gives the standards, the exact model (51.5° N, ±23.44°, sun time) and the named misconceptions.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 and desktop screenshots of every step before and after Show me (/workspace/shots-0751/sun-ph-*, sun-p3-*, sun-d-*, sun-d3-*). Fixes after the first pass: the midday Sun overlapped the place label (sky scale lowered), end labels of the clock strip were clipped (now left/right aligned), stars were drawn in diagonal lines (now scattered), and the month label overlapped the North Pole tag on wide screens (moved into a chip by the Sun; globe smaller). The strip handle is 24 px across and the whole canvas drags the clock; every action has a button.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all four tasks complete with Show me, challenge shown, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes, no console errors. Every drag has a button (− 1 hour, + 1 hour, Play the whole day, June, December, Spin one day, three bin buttons). The canvas aria-label gives the place, time, whether the Sun is up, hours watched and hours of light, or the pole and home light state after a spin, and messages are spoken with c.say.
